rationale: The selected chip differs from unselected chips ONLY by its fill color (blue #1a73e8 vs grey #e8eaed); there is no checkmark, no border-shape change, no bold, and no text token. Rendered in grayscale the selected chip is no longer distinguishable, so selection is conveyed by color alone.
citation: SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element."

rationale: The invalid field signals its error state ONLY by turning its border red (#d93025 vs neutral #5f6368); there is no error icon, no error message, and no border-style change. Per F81/TT an error indicator cannot use color alone, and in grayscale the field appears valid.
citation: Failure F81: "Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.1 due to identifying required or error fields using color differences only."

rationale: Required fields are distinguished from optional ones ONLY by the label being rendered red (#d93025); there is no asterisk, no "(required)" text, and no glyph. The required-ness is conveyed by color difference alone, which F81 names directly.
citation: Failure F81: "Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.1 due to identifying required or error fields using color differences only."

rationale: The toggle's only on/off cue is the track color (green #34a853 on vs grey #cccccc off). There is no ON/OFF text, no icon, and the knob is fixed at left:4px in both states so there is no position cue. In grayscale the on and off tracks are nearly indistinguishable; state is color only.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" (and shape/position) — required because color is the sole on/off signal here.

rationale: The selected table row is distinguished from other rows ONLY by a faint background tint (#e8f0fe on white); there is no checkmark cell, no bold text, no border emphasis, and no "selected" label. In grayscale the tint nearly vanishes, so row selection is conveyed by color alone.
citation: SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element."

rationale: The current tab is signaled ONLY by blue text (#1a73e8), and the SAME blue is the :hover color, so when an inactive tab is hovered it becomes visually identical to the current tab. There is no underline, no bold, and no bottom-border. The current state is conveyed by color alone and is ambiguous in the hovered state.
citation: SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element."

rationale: The actively-sorted column is indicated ONLY by its header text turning blue (#1a73e8); there is no ascending/descending arrow glyph and no "(sorted)" text, so neither which column drives the sort nor the direction is available without color. In grayscale no sorted column is identifiable.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" — the sort indicator must not be color-only.

rationale: Completed steps differ from upcoming steps ONLY by circle fill color (green #34a853 vs grey #cccccc); there is no checkmark drawn inside the dot, no "Done" text, and no shape change. In grayscale completed and upcoming dots look alike, so completion status is color only.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" (or shape) — completion must not be signaled by fill color alone.

rationale: Today's date cell is distinguished from other days ONLY by a blue background fill (#1a73e8 with white text); there is no ring/border, no "Today" caption, no bold weight, and no shape difference. In grayscale today is no longer identifiable, so current-day status is conveyed by color alone.
citation: SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element."

rationale: The custom checkbox shows ONLY a fill-color change when checked (blue box vs white box) while keeping the same square shape, size, and border weight; no tick/checkmark is rendered. In grayscale the checked and unchecked boxes are nearly identical, so checked state is conveyed by fill color alone.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" (or shape) — the checked state needs a non-color cue such as a tick.

rationale: The selected segment carries aria-selected="true", which is PROGRAMMATIC and satisfies 4.1.2/1.3.1 but is NOT a visual cue. Its only VISIBLE difference is the blue fill (#1a73e8 vs #f1f3f4) — no bold, no underline, no checkmark, no border. Because 1.4.1 is about the VISUAL presentation, aria alone does NOT rescue it; in grayscale the selection disappears, so this is still a 1.4.1 failure.
citation: SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information ... or distinguishing a visual element." (ARIA state is programmatic, not a visual means.)

rationale: The invalid status is conveyed by swapping a background-IMAGE (a raster icon) plus a red border, with no onscreen text or markup glyph. The truth is a failure (color/raster only, no classifiable onscreen cue), but a static analyzer cannot read inside the bitmap to determine whether it carries non-color meaning, so the runner should abstain rather than decide.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1.3 (13.A): "An error indicator cannot use color alone as an indicator." / "Displaying content in grayscale may help identify content that uses only color."

rationale: The selected chip is blue AND carries an onscreen "Selected" text token that unselected chips lack. The visible text label conveys selection independent of color, so in grayscale the selected chip remains identifiable by its label — passes.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" — satisfied by the persistent onscreen "Selected" text.

rationale: The checked custom checkbox fills blue AND draws an onscreen "✓" checkmark inside the box. The tick is a shape cue present whenever checked and independent of color, so the checked state survives grayscale — passes.
citation: Technique G182 / G14: ensuring information conveyed by color is also available without color (here a checkmark shape) — satisfied.

rationale: The current tab is blue AND gains a 3px solid bottom-border underline that hovered inactive tabs never get. The thick bottom-border is a non-color shape/weight cue, so even when another tab is hovered the current tab stays distinguishable in grayscale — passes.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available" via shape/border — satisfied by the underline bar.

rationale: Today's cell is blue AND has a visible onscreen "•" dot glyph beneath the number plus a 2px ring, with aria-current also present. The dot and ring are onscreen non-color cues, so today remains identifiable in grayscale — passes (the aria-current is supplementary, not the load-bearing cue).
citation: Technique G182: "Ensuring that additional visual cues are available when text color differences are used" — satisfied by the dot glyph and ring.

rationale: The switch shows onscreen "ON"/"OFF" text AND the knob slides to the right when checked (a position cue). Track color is redundant; on/off is conveyed by both visible text and knob position, so the state survives grayscale — passes.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" (and by position) — satisfied by ON/OFF text and knob travel.

rationale: The invalid field turns red AND shows a persistent ONSCREEN error message ("Enter a valid email address") plus a "⚠" warning glyph. The message is rendered (not mouse-over-only), so the error is conveyed without relying on color and survives grayscale — passes.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1.3 (13.A): "another visual, onscreen method is used to convey the information which does not use color." (The onscreen error text is not mouse-over-only.)

rationale: The selected list row is tinted AND its text becomes bold with an underline, while unselected rows are normal weight. Font-weight and underline are color-independent cues, so the selected row stays distinguishable in grayscale — passes.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available" via text styling (bold/underline) — satisfied.

rationale: Required fields carry an explicit onscreen "(required)" text token (the red asterisk is paired with the word), so required-ness is conveyed by text regardless of color and survives grayscale — passes.
citation: Technique G14: "Ensuring that information conveyed by color differences is also available in text" — satisfied by the onscreen "(required)" word.

rationale: Both validity states carry a distinct onscreen glyph (green "✓" when valid, red "✗" when invalid) in addition to color. The two glyph shapes differ from each other, so valid vs invalid is distinguishable without relying on green vs red and survives grayscale in every state — passes.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1.3 (13.A): "another visual, onscreen method is used to convey the information which does not use color." — the per-state glyphs satisfy this in each state.

rationale: The hover tint is a purely decorative pointer affordance; it encodes no status, selection, validity, or required-ness — no information is conveyed by the color change. SC 1.4.1 only applies when color CONVEYS information, so this decorative-only hover is exempt — passes.
citation: SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information ..." — applies only where color conveys information; a decorative hover tint conveys none.

rationale: The selected chip turns blue AND reveals an inline SVG that visually renders a checkmark — a genuine onscreen non-color shape cue, so the case truly PASSES. But the bare SVG path has no title/role and a static analyzer cannot prove it conveys "selected" versus being decorative, so the runner should abstain rather than decide.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1.3 (13.A): "another visual, onscreen method is used to convey the information which does not use color." — an unlabeled SVG glyph is onscreen but not statically classifiable.
